name: Kern
title: Kern (1.1.2)
lifecycleNote: v1.1.2 (2026-10-28) is the newest published stable release; a v1.2.0 tag exists on the development line with its release pipeline still failing at assessment

presenceList.meta: R2, Ec3, Ec8, V1, V5, L1

tagline: Capabilities in the Signature, Europe in the Supply

type.text: **I/O authority is a parameter, and the compiler enforces it**: every authority-bearing call demands a `Cap<T>` argument in the signature, ambient authority is the compile error E0404 with no off switch, only `@cap_constructor` functions mint, and the entry module mints the roots — a function that cannot show a `Cap<Fs>` cannot read a file, which puts the effect where the caller reads it

**Nullability, exhaustiveness and boundaries are type facts**: `str` is never null and `str?` is the opt-in with flow-sensitive narrowing; unions carry payloads and `match` must cover every variant; `pub` and the enforced import list (E0327) are a real module boundary; conversions are named calls (`int()`, `float()`) with no implicit narrowing, and `bool` and `int` are distinct

**Functions are coloured by declaration, not by kind**: `await` composes inside a plain `fn` body — every example on the async page awaits tasks from a `fn main` — so the `async fn` marker does not spread through the call graph the way a second function kind does elsewhere

**Generic type parameters are erased**: every generic parameter compiles to an opaque `i8*`, and integer and float values are boxed crossing generic code; there is no reflection API to reach structure at run time, so the charge is the erasure half — the artifact no longer carries the type argument, as on the TypeScript page

**The systems profile crosses to raw memory and syscalls**: a `@nogc` function, or every function in a `@systems` file, may call the `__mem_*` and `__syscall` intrinsics, and `std.cap_unsafe` hands out `Cap<Unsafe>` raw addresses — layout, lifetime and the syscall ABI are hand-written agreements the type system does not check, and the memory-safe guarantee stops at that crossing

**`length` is named characters and ships bytes**: the string module's docstring reads 'Returns the number of characters in the string', and the runtime source states `kern_str_length` returns 'the byte-length of a string (excluding NUL)'; the codepoint count ships under a different name (`str.char_count`, pure Kern, continuation bytes skipped), `reverse()` has been codepoint-aware since 1.0.0, and `char_at` and `slice` index positions whose unit the reference does not state

construction.text: **State is local and immutable unless written down**: bindings are immutable without `mut`, structs are immutable without `type mut`, construction names every field with required fields enforced (E0207) and declared defaults, and every declaration carries its initialiser in the grammar — no value exists off a path that filled it

**The default map is a hash table with no order promise**: `Map<K, V>` is FNV-1a with chaining and resize at 75% load, `keys()` states no order, and the library ships no ordered sibling — code that assembles output, a payload or a report from an iteration agrees with a hash function

**Mutable heap values alias by default**: structs are heap-allocated and a `type mut` struct's fields mutate through every alias, with the alias set undeclared; `list_append` appends in place and returns the same list — the reference itself records that 'several stdlib modules that promise immutability silently mutated their caller's data' until the behaviour was written down

**Module-level initialisers run once at program start, in declaration order — within a module**: the specification states no order across modules for an initialiser that reads another module's module-level state, and no rule for a cycle; the create-once constant the race check steers toward (`const REQUESTS = atomic_new(0)`) stays inside one module, but the cross-module read is the loader's sequence

memory.text: **A tracing mark-and-sweep collector owns the heap**: stop-the-world and ThreadSanitizer-checked, with per-request epoch GC on the HTTP path — memory returns when the collector decides, not when the last reference goes
**No ownership model**: the collector owns every heap object and no type records who may free or mutate; the `mut` mark says the value can change, not who may change it

**The fatal classes sit outside the declared surface**: `panic`, `.unwrap()` on an `Err`, a failed `assert`, and overflow-checked arithmetic that 'aborts the program with a diagnostic' are faults no catch reaches — the declared failure path is the `Result` value, and these end the program by design

**Release and reclamation have named forms**: `defer` schedules a call at scope exit, `weak_new` holds a reference the collector may clear, cycles are collected, and no `malloc`/`free` exists in Kern code

**The trusted base is C**: roughly 42,000 budget-capped lines with a written ledger, ThreadSanitizer on the synchronisation primitives, and a stated programme to shrink it — the memory-safe story stops at the runtime's own boundary

error.text: **Failures are values end to end**: there are no exceptions; `Result<T, E>` carries any error type, `?` propagates only where the enclosing function declares the same `E`, `match` is exhaustive, and a `-> never` function ends a block for the return analysis

**A discarded failure is silence**: match is exhaustive where it is used and `?` propagates, but no diagnostic stops a `Result`-valued call from standing as a statement, the Go-shaped `content, err = fs.read(path)` pair leaves the `if err:` to the programmer, `.unwrap()` trades the check for a crash, and `str_to_int` returns 0 for input it cannot read

concurrency.text: **Mutability is the mark the race check reads**: a `mut` module global written from concurrent code — a spawn target, an HTTP handler or middleware, a `service` impl method, or anything they call, including the body of a spawned lambda — is the compile error E0309, so the default is not unchecked sharing

**A race class is detected at compile time**: E0309 rejects the unsynchronised concurrent write; the scope is the checker's own — module globals and what concurrent code reaches — and container read-modify-write is a W0005 warning in the default edition, becoming E0309 only under edition 2027

**A spawned task is joined by hand**: `spawn` returns a handle, `await all` joins an explicit list, and no construct scopes a task's lifetime to a block — a scope can end while work it started still runs

**The concurrency kit is first-class**: cooperative routines on a libuv loop with per-coroutine preemption, dedicated `spawn_thread` for CPU-bound and blocking work, channels with a required capacity (0 is a rendezvous), mutex, RWLock, semaphore, atomics, and `select` — a routine that awaits parks, never an OS thread

**The 1.1.x line shipped with concurrency defects its own changelog names**: a cooperative `Mutex<T>` that could freeze the scheduler thread when a holder was descheduled (fixed in 1.1.2), the same defect in `RwLock<T>` documented as unfixed at this release, and multi-worker `await` windows — 'avoid `KERN_WORKERS` > 0 in production until v1.1.3'

platform.text: **One implementation is the language**: a self-hosted compiler with no second front end, one vendor's release calendar, and no independent implementation to compare against — the working reality is one toolchain
**The artifact is a single static native binary**: LLVM to the named target triple, no runtime loaded at run time, and therefore no runtime/program version skew to manage — the upgrade is a rebuild

performance.text: **Collector pauses are in the timing budget**: stop-the-world marking bounds the pause and does not remove it; per-request epoch GC keeps a request's collection local, and the schedule is still the runtime's

**Ahead-of-time native, no JIT tier**: LLVM emits the binary the machine runs, so cold starts carry no warm-up; the project's own 55-workload matrix against Go, Node, Python, Rust and C states its losses (file I/O, hashing) beside its wins, with per-cell ceilings — self-reported, not independent

ecosystem.text: **The supply is one vendor's**: 309 standard-library modules and ten first-party packages against a third-party pool measured in single repositories — zero stars and two watchers on the forge at assessment — so more is written than found, and hiring follows the same curve

**The standard library is the platform by design**: HTTP, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Redis, JSON, crypto, containers and a microVM monitor ship in-tree, so the concentration the supply and implementation criteria price is a deliberate trade — the dependency tree that would diversify the supply is the thing the design avoids, and that choice is charged under `Ec3` and `P2`, not as a community framework monoculture

**The runtime bundle crosses as a binary with the promise set to nothing**: published so a build can skip roughly 36,000 lines of C, version-paired by convention, with the stability policy stating the C runtime's symbol names 'are NOT part of the stable surface' and can change between minor versions; the v1.1.1 bundle linked on an mbedTLS-2.28 host and SIGSEGVd at the first TLS use, and 1.1.2's answer — per-ABI bundles and a build-time soname gate (E0504) — is a check at link, not a promise

evolution.text: **The stable line has already broken code, by its own documented exception**: 1.0.3 landed in a patch release with nine host-state functions retyped to take `Cap<Container>` — 'BREAKING for direct importers' — removed `std.ai`, and moved runtime internals behind E0408, under the stability policy's rule that closing a fail-open path is a fix even when a program depended on it; elsewhere the frozen corpus is compiled on every change, and edition 2027's three promotions wait for an opt-in

**What changed: two isolation defaults moved within the stable line.** 1.0.2 made the allowlist the default process-container seccomp profile, where the previous default allowed everything not on a denylist; 1.0.3 defaulted `KERN_VM_DATAPATH` to vhost and refuses to start a guest when it cannot be opened rather than falling back. Why: fail-closed isolation defaults. How a deployment reverses it: `InstanceSpec.seccomp` set to `denylist` per instance, and `KERN_VM_DATAPATH=user`; both are documented per release, and the stability policy reserves the right to move tuning-knob defaults

domain.text: **The target is ordinary backend service work**: registered handlers are plain functions, a `service` block generates the RPC plumbing from a typed interface, and the deployment unit is one static binary — no host framework owns the program's shape

learning.text: **The capability discipline is the language**: every I/O function threads a `Cap<T>`, only the entry module mints roots, taint tags decide which sinks accept which values, and failures arrive as values to match or propagate — a compile-time discipline with no mainstream analogue in the daily syntax, however Python-like the surface reads

**The official reference is strong, and has drifted**: a normative specification with the grammar embedded from a canonical file, a 72 KB diagnostics catalogue with one page per code, and per-module references are far above the pre-1.0 norm — and the async page's own summary table still shows `ch.send(...)` method forms its body says do not exist, while the spec's governance paragraph describes an elected technical committee the governing documents do not name

testing.text: **The verification path ships with the compiler**: `kern test` is stable CLI, `assert`/`assert_eq`/`assert_ne` are builtins, `## kern-time:` declares a test's run-time budget, fuzz targets run in CI, DWARF is emitted for the standard debuggers, and the LSP answers from the real typechecker

security.text: **The exploit classes are named and closed in the type**: memory-safe managed runtime with no `eval`; injection sinks demand literals (`@sql_literal` E0300, `@shell_literal`, `@url_literal`, `@regex_literal`) or an `Untrusted<T>` discharge; a `Secret` compared with `==` is the compile error E0317; and overflow arithmetic aborts rather than wrapping

**The guarantee is young, and its holes are documented by the project**: the rc3 external scan found method arguments never type-checked, so every compile-time security rule was bypassable by ordinary idiomatic code; 1.0.3 closed capability bypasses that reached 203 gated builtins, a world-readable container state root carrying env values, and state-record field injection; and the formal proofs cover models — only the lexer's model is measured against the shipped code, the taint model has no heap, aliasing or concurrency, and the external audit was removed from the plan

reproducibility.text: **Byte-reproducible by gate, not by aspiration**: the same source, toolchain version and seed give a byte-identical binary, asserted on every push by rebuilding a clean-room compiler from the minimal seed and comparing two full bootstraps (seed to gen1 to gen2), with diverse double-compilation alongside

**The resolution is a function of the manifests**: Minimal Version Selection pins the whole transitive graph in `kern.lock`, and `kern.sum` carries two content hashes per version, trust-on-first-use and then immutable; `.kern-version` beside the source makes the compiler warn when a different toolchain builds it

supplychain.text: **Packages are signed, checksummed and fail-closed**: `kern-pkg verify` refuses a missing hash line, a mismatch, or an unverifiable signature; publishing packs byte-reproducible tarballs; release tags and artefacts are signed with keys whose public halves are pinned in the repository

**The registry name space is flat**: names like `kern-postgres` resolve on the forge's generic package registry with the owner a publish credential rather than a namespace in the module path — substitution is answered by the hash-and-signature verification, not by the name space

**No advisory feed joins vulnerabilities to package versions**: `kern audit` exists in the CLI and the dependency documentation names no database behind it; the 1.0.3 security release's own advisory was still 'to be published at coordinated disclosure' at this tag

observability.text: **The stdlib defines the contract**: structured logging, latency metrics, W3C tracing and health checks ship in-tree, with `kern_otel` as the OpenTelemetry package — no per-project instrumentation convention is required

**A crash documents no post-mortem**: the reference and release notes document no default backtrace with source locations — the FATAL diagnostic line is the crash's printed record, and the forensic record-replay trace and the async wedge trace are env-gated opt-ins

feedback.text: **Compile speed is a stated design goal with its own programme**: the compiler bootstraps from source in seconds and the project carries a go-parity matrix with per-cell ceilings — the project's own measurements, not an independent one

**No debugger ships with the toolchain**: the CLI is build, check, fix, lint, test, new, explain, audit-caps, bootstrap, version — DWARF is emitted for the standard debuggers, which the distribution does not include

interop.text: **The foreign surface exists in-process**: the `@nogc` intrinsics, `std.cap_unsafe` raw addresses, and the C runtime the compiler links are reachable without leaving the language — the charge is the boundary being unchecked (T14), not its absence

**No portable target ships at this release**: the normative spec's target table lists WebAssembly as 'Future' and the v1.1.2 README names none — the project website's wasm32-wasip1 row tracks the newer line, not the assessed release

governance.text: **PUA Group decides**: breaking, governance and licence changes are the company's decision after a public review period, releases are cut by a maintainer acting on its behalf — and the spec's own governance paragraph, 'no single corporate owner, decisions made by elected technical committee', describes a body the governing documents do not name

**The specification is public and normative**: a 72 KB document that defines the stable surface, embeds the grammar verbatim from a canonical file a CI gate keeps in sync, and states its stability policy as a contract with named tests beside each claim

**The oracle is one toolchain**: the conformance and negative suites are the implementation's own, no published suite exists for an independent implementation to run, and the project states the limit itself — the capability and flow models are proved about models, with the 54-probe grid as the evidence the shipped checker implements them, and the external audit removed from the plan
**The compiler is the published parser**: the source is EUPL and the canonical grammar lives in the tree, with a CI gate failing on drift between grammar and specification

tradeoffs: **The type system is the seccomp profile**: the compiler derives a seccomp-BPF deny set from the program's `Cap<T>` mint set and emits the kernel seal first in `@main`, inherited across `execve` — Linux only, no-op on macOS

**Forensic record-replay is opt-in and env-gated**: `KERN_RECORD`/`KERN_REPLAY` capture and re-feed the nondeterministic values the runtime hands the program under a SHA-256 chain that detects an edited trace — bought with per-record capture overhead and an operator's decision to run traced, which is why it is a deployment tool and not a default

**Closures are single-expression by rule**: multi-line request handlers are named functions registered on a route — the parser never guesses a body's extent inside an expression, and the multi-line logic lands in a named, testable function, paid in a line of ceremony per handler

**The manifest accepts unknown keys in silence**: a section or key the `kern.toml` parser does not know is read past with no warning — the lenient read keeps a manifest carrying newer keys building on an older toolchain, and costs a typo'd key that sits in the file looking effective and doing nothing, as the documentation itself warns for `[runtime]` and `authors`
**Reserved names carry the runtime**: the `kern_` prefix is refused for user functions (E0405) precisely so the C symbol set can move between minor versions

**Shadowing a builtin is module-scoped**: a function defined with a builtin's name wins in its own module and its importers, and reaches the builtin through its capability wrapper — one of the two naming rules the reference says 'trip newcomers'
verdict: Kern's Core coupling (76.0) lands above every managed mainstream neighbour assessed so far, because the inventory's rarest absences are its design facts: effects in the signature (`Cap<T>` under an unconditional E0404), nullability in the type, errors as exhaustive values, immutability by default, overflow trapped rather than wrapped, cycles collected, `defer` at scope exit, and a public normative specification. What it keeps is the managed-runtime invoice — the collector's schedule and pauses, erased generics, aliased mutable heap state, an unordered map, join-by-hand tasks — plus its own additions: a fatal class (panic, unwrap, overflow) outside the declared `Result` surface, and a length API that names characters and ships bytes. Its youth is priced where youth lives: a one-vendor supply and governance, a single implementation as the only oracle, a flat registry name space, no portable target at this release, no bundled debugger, no documented crash post-mortem, and no advisory feed. The page records what the project documents about itself, which is unusually much: the changelog names its own security holes and known memory-safety defects, the stability policy states which promises are not made, and the formal-scope page draws the line between proved models and shipped code. Main strengths: capability tracking the type carries, and a verification culture — reproducible, double-compiled, signed, specified — that outpaces the language's age. Main weaknesses: everything below the Core score is time — supply, independent governance, a second implementation, an advisory base — and those are not bought in a first year.

energy.text: Compiles ahead of time to native code via LLVM, so the interpreter-tax class does not apply; the runtime pays stop-the-world collector pauses and drives a libuv event loop. The project's own benchmark matrix (55 backend workloads against Go, Node.js, Python, Rust and C, losses stated beside wins) reports its methodology and date; independent measurements do not yet exist.

ai-readiness.text: Sparse corpus: the first stable release (2026-10-03) postdates the training data of public coding models, and the project's own documentation records model-shaped inventions that do not exist — a `parse_int` builtin, `items.map`, `ch.send` — so models write plausible Kern that the compiler refuses. The per-code diagnostics catalogue and `kern explain E0xxx` are the compensation.

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems. The systems profile (`@nogc`, a deterministic arena allocator, bounds-checked DMA windows, a locked systems surface) targets hypervisor-class software rather than a certification regime, and the formal proofs cover models — the lexer-to-compiler correspondence is measured, the capability and flow links rest on a probe grid.

delivery.note: Published so a build can skip roughly 36,000 lines of C, version-paired by release convention; the stability policy states a 1.x program links the runtime shipped with 1.x and that the C runtime's symbol names are not part of the stable surface, so no cross-release pairing is promised. The v1.1.1 bundle linked on an mbedTLS-2.28 host and SIGSEGVd at the first TLS use; 1.1.2 answers with per-ABI bundles and a build-time soname gate (E0504) — a check at link, which the criteria do not treat as a promise

Packages ship as source tarballs built inside the consumer's own build — nothing crosses, so no release promise is at stake; `kern.lock` and `kern.sum` pin the resolved graph by content hash and the Ed25519 `kern.trust` path verifies signatures fail-closed
The deployed artifact is a single static binary consumed whole — the stability policy states no Kern runtime is loaded at run time, and no plugin or shared-object surface ships, so nothing crosses

data_formats.note: The lock and the content-hash database are documented formats enforced fail-closed on install and verify; `kern.sum` entries are trust-on-first-use and then immutable

The store is versioned (v28, v29) and the changelog documents upgrade-ahead skew handling: counters read as -1 defaults when a newer plane reads an older host, and an unknown journal entry boots as a no-op with a warning
The stability policy publishes the wire format (JSON over gRPC) as stable within a major version: a 1.a client talks to a 1.b server
